text:
On a hundred items, almost any code is fast. The interview question is what it costs at a million, and which structure keeps it cheap. Thirty-five questions, argued with counts, not code: eight with a figure each, three inside those, and twenty-four quickly.

Question one. What is Big-O notation, and why do interviewers care? It says how time or memory grows with the input size, n, ignoring constants. A double loop over a hundred items checks under five thousand pairs. Instant. At a million items, it's half a trillion. Model it at a hundred million checks a second, an assumption: about eighty-three minutes. One pass over the million: a hundredth of a second. That's why they care: Big-O predicts whether a solution survives its real input. The usual game is turning a brute-force n squared into n. But constants are dropped, so at a hundred items the brute force is often fine, and simpler. Say what it costs, and where it stops being fine.

Question two. When do you reach for a hash map? When you need lookups and inserts by key in constant time on average: counting, grouping, have I seen this? It turns Two Sum's double loop into one pass: at each number, ask the map for target minus it, then store the number. Linear time, at the cost of linear memory. Average is the key word. With a thousand buckets, a shared bucket is more likely than not by the thirty-eighth key. The follow-up is the worst case. Give a thousand keys the same hash, and filling a Python set takes nearly six hundred thousand key comparisons. With distinct hashes, none. That's a hash set: constant on average, linear space, and linear per operation at worst.
